title: Metrics
body:
The attempt to put numbers on software so that quality and progress can be argued about with
evidence rather than opinion. Two families:

**Process metrics** measure the project: effort spent, schedule slip, defects found per
phase, cost to fix a defect at each stage of the [[SDLC]]. These are what
[[Project Success]] is judged against.

**Product metrics** measure the artefact: lines of code, [[Complexity]] (in the software
sense, e.g. counting the branches through a function), depth of an inheritance hierarchy,
coupling counts between modules. See [[Coupling and Cohesion]].

The catch is worth remembering: **a metric that becomes a target stops measuring what it
measured.** Lines of code is the standard example. As a rough size estimate it is fine; as a
productivity target it rewards writing more code to do the same thing, which is the opposite
of the goal. The same trap catches defect counts (report fewer) and test coverage (write
tests that execute lines without asserting anything).

So metrics are useful for spotting *trends and outliers*, a module whose coupling count is
five times its neighbours' is worth a [[Review]], and unreliable as a scoreboard. Related:
[[Code Smells]], which is the same signal read qualitatively instead of numerically.
